title: Checkpoints: undo anything
content:
## What you'll get

Every change is saved automatically as a checkpoint. You can jump back to any earlier version, try risky experiments safely, or even split your project into two parallel versions - all without losing a single line of code.

## How automatic checkpoints work

Emergent saves a **snapshot** every time the agent finishes working or you manually save. Think of these as checkpoints in a video game - you can always go back to one if something goes wrong.

<Callout type="note" title="Nothing is ever lost">
Your current state is preserved before any rollback completes, so you can always roll forward again if you change your mind.
</Callout>

<Callout type="info" title="Screenshot coming soon">
Screenshot of the History panel showing the timeline of snapshots will be added.
</Callout>

## Going back to an earlier version

If the agent breaks something - maybe it removed a button, deleted files you need, or misunderstood an instruction - you can **rollback** to a point when everything worked.

<Steps>
<Step title="Open your history">
In the workspace, click the **History** icon in the left sidebar. You'll see a timeline of snapshots - each one represents a save point.
</Step>

<Step title="Preview what changed">
Click any earlier snapshot to see exactly what changed between that point and now. Files added, modified, or deleted are highlighted so you can spot the problem.
</Step>

<Step title="Confirm the rollback">
Click **Rollback to this version**. The platform restores all your code, settings, and configuration from that snapshot and redeploys the app automatically. Your current state gets saved as a new snapshot labeled "Before rollback" - nothing disappears.
</Step>
</Steps>

The app restarts on its own. Your deployment URL stays exactly the same.

<Callout type="info" title="Video coming soon">
A short screen recording of the rollback process will go here.
</Callout>

## Experimenting without risk: forking

Sometimes you don't want to undo - you want to **try something big** without touching your working app. That's what **forking** is for.

Forking creates a complete, independent copy of your app. The original keeps running; the copy (the "fork") becomes a separate project where you can experiment freely.

<Steps>
<Step title="Open the app menu">
Click the app name dropdown or the three-dot menu next to your app title in the workspace header.
</Step>

<Step title="Select Fork">
Choose **Fork App**. The platform duplicates your entire app - code, database structure, chat history - into a new project.
</Step>

<Step title="Name your experiment">
Give the fork a clear name like "MyApp - Redesign Test" so you remember what it's for.
</Step>

<Step title="Build independently">
The fork appears as its own project. Chat, build, and deploy in the fork without affecting the original. If the experiment works, keep the fork. If it fails, just delete it and go back to the original.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="tip" title="Fork before risky changes">
Thinking of asking the agent to "refactor the entire backend"? Fork first. If things go sideways, you haven't lost anything.
</Callout>

### What gets copied when you fork

- **All your code and files** at the moment of the fork
- **Database structure** (tables, indexes) - but not the actual data rows, so the fork starts with an empty database
- **Chat history** up to the fork point, so the agent remembers why the code exists
- **Build settings** and non-secret environment variables

<Callout type="warning" title="Secrets aren't copied">
API keys and secret tokens don't copy over for security reasons. You'll need to re-add any required secrets in the forked app's settings before deploying.
</Callout>

## Rollback vs. fork: when to use each

| You want to... | Use |
|----------------|-----|
| Undo a recent bad change | **Rollback** |
| Try a big experiment without touching the working app | **Fork** |
| Build a variant for a different customer or use case | **Fork** |
| Recover from multiple mistakes over time | Rollback to a known-good state, *then* fork if you want to explore a different direction in parallel |

<Callout type="info" title="Think of it this way">
Rollback is "undo." Forking is "duplicate and diverge."
</Callout>

## If something looks wrong after rolling back

Rollback restores your code, dependencies, settings, and database structure - but it **doesn't change your actual data**. If the old code expects the database to look different than it does now, you might see errors until you manually clean up or adjust the data.

<Callout type="note" title="What rollback includes">
✅ All source code files  
✅ Dependencies and packages  
✅ Environment variables  
✅ Build configuration  
✅ Database schema (table structures, indexes)

❌ Database data (your actual records stay as-is)  
❌ External API keys stored outside the platform  
❌ Custom domain DNS records
</Callout>

Always test your app after a rollback to make sure critical features still work.
description: Every change is saved automatically. Go back anytime - nothing is ever lost.
